title: Asking forgiveness

lines: THE NEXT PART ISN'T UP TO HIM.
cards: A man stands on a doorstep with his hand raised to knock. On the drive over he rehearsed three versions, each a little shorter. His heart is going faster than it did at his job interview.
Inside is a friend he hasn't spoken to since the night he said the thing. Nothing is stopping him from knocking, except that once he does, the next part isn't up to him. Forgiving happens inside you.
Asking puts it in somebody else's hands. Today: asking forgiveness.

teach.h: THE HOLY DAY CAN'T ASK FOR YOU.

teach.b: The Mishnah, in its tractate on Yom Kippur, teaches that the Day of Atonement covers wrongs between a person and God, but wrongs between people aren't covered until you make peace with the person you wronged.
The holiest day can't do the asking for you, and neither can a prayer said alone or a good intention kept to yourself.
Some Jewish families keep a custom of asking one another's forgiveness in the days before Yom Kippur for exactly this reason. Second, the rehearsal.

teach.h: A SPEECH REHEARSED ON THE ROAD.
teach.b: In Luke's story of the prodigal son, the younger son, broke and hungry, plans his speech on the way home: "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee." He even plans to ask to be taken on as a hired servant.
That's the man at the door with three versions. Third, what happens.

teach.h: HIS FATHER SAW HIM, AND RAN.
teach.b: Luke says: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran." The son starts his speech, and the father cuts it short with a robe and a ring. The hired-servant line never gets said.
The courage was in the walking home; the speech mattered less than he thought.

teach.h: THE ANSWER ISN'T YOURS TO CONTROL.

teach.b: Not every door opens like that one. The other person may say no, or not yet. That's why it takes nerve: you walk up the path without knowing the answer, and say the two plain words.

how: Some Jewish families ask one another for forgiveness in the days before Yom Kippur, and Christians often read the prodigal son in Luke 15 as a picture of coming home to ask forgiveness.

o: owning a wrong to the person, and leaving their answer to them
a formal ritual that cancels the wrong once it's said
waiting for the other person to come and apologize first

games.q: who teaches what — tap the pairs.
p: make peace with the person first
sees him far off, and runs

s: the Mishnah teaches that Yom Kippur covers every wrong, including wrongs against people
wrongs between people aren't covered until you make peace with the person you wronged.
in Luke, the father runs to his son while he's still a great way off
"when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran."
the prodigal son gets to finish his whole rehearsed speech
his father cuts it short with a robe and a ring; the hired-servant line never gets said.

games.q: you're the younger son, walking home, broke, with your speech ready. your father sees you far off. what does Luke say happens next?
o: he waits at the door to hear the whole speech.
he runs to you before you reach the house.
he sends a servant to ask what you want.
games.why: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran." the speech gets cut short with a robe and a ring.

practice: Let one person come to mind whom you'd like to ask for forgiveness, someone safe to approach, for something you can honestly own.

Notice what your body does at the thought, the tight chest, the urge to explain, and find a first sentence that's short and has no excuses in it. Say it silently, twice, and if you pray, ask for courage in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Asking forgiveness. Owning a wrong to the person you wronged, and leaving their answer in their hands. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: I'm sorry. Two plain words, with no "but" after them. See you tomorrow.
